items.title: Google rolls out Nano Banana 2 as default AI image model across Gemini

featured_image.name: Google launches Nano Banana Pro powered by Gemini 3 - CNBC

items.description:
Google on Thursday unveiled Nano Banana 2, the latest version of its viral AI image generation tool, rolling it out as the default image model across the Gemini app, Google Search, and its video editing tool Flow. Officially designated Gemini 3.1 Flash Image, the upgrade brings capabilities previously reserved for the higher-end Nano Banana Pro model to a broader audience at faster speeds.[1][2]

The new model produces images with resolutions ranging from 512 pixels to 4K across multiple aspect ratios, supports character consistency for up to five characters, and can maintain fidelity of up to 14 objects in a single workflow, according to TechCrunch. It also inherits Nano Banana Pro's advanced world knowledge, accurate text rendering, and the ability to generate data visualizations and infographics — features that made the Pro version popular among creators and professionals.[3][2][1]

items.title: NASA-backed study turns recycled sewage into lunar and Martian crop fertilizer

featured_image.name: Interstellar soil science: Aggie researcher explores farming on Mars

items.description:
Researchers working with NASA have demonstrated that recycled human and plant waste can be combined with simulated lunar and Martian soil to release nutrients essential for growing crops, a step toward making off-world agriculture sustainable for future space colonies.

The study, published in ACS Earth and Space Chemistry and highlighted in a press release this week by the American Chemical Society, describes how a nutrient-dense solution derived from processed sewage was mixed with materials designed to mimic the rocky, barren surfaces of the moon and Mars. The interaction released plant-essential elements including sulfur, calcium, and magnesium, offering early evidence that waste recycling could transform lifeless extraterrestrial terrain into something approaching farmable soil.[1][2]

items.title: US, Ukraine meet in Geneva after Russia's massive overnight aerial barrage

featured_image.name: US, Ukraine to meet in Geneva after overnight Russian ...

items.description:
Ukraine's lead negotiator Rustem Umerov was set to meet US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Geneva on Thursday for bilateral talks focused on Ukraine's postwar economic recovery and preparations for a new round of trilateral negotiations with Russia expected in early March. The meeting came just hours after Russia launched one of its largest aerial assaults in months, firing 420 drones and 39 missiles at targets across eight Ukrainian regions overnight.[1][2]

The Geneva session marks the latest effort by the Trump administration to maintain diplomatic momentum as the war enters its fifth year, with both sides still deadlocked over the fate of Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory.

items.title: US and Iran hold critical nuclear talks as Trump's deadline nears

featured_image.name: Iran's Araghchi arrives in Geneva for second round of nuclear talks with US

items.description:
Iran and the United States are set to hold a third round of indirect nuclear negotiations in Geneva on Thursday, in what both sides and outside observers describe as a last-ditch diplomatic effort to prevent a military confrontation. The talks come amid a massive American military buildup in the Middle East and just days before a deadline set by President Donald Trump for Tehran to accept a deal on its nuclear program.[1][2][3][4]

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who arrived in Geneva on Wednesday night, will lead Iran's delegation, while White House envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner will represent the American side. As in prior rounds, Oman's Foreign Minister Badr al-Busaidi is serving as an intermediary, shuttling proposals between the two delegations, which are not meeting face to face.[3][4][5]

items.title: Magnetic microrobot swarms move objects without touching them

featured_image.name: Swarming microrobots use spinning flows to turn gears without touching

items.description:
Swarms of tiny magnetic robots can now rotate, transport, and assemble objects thousands of times their own mass — all without making physical contact. In a study published this week in Science Advances, researchers from the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, the University of Michigan, and Cornell University demonstrated that coordinated groups of spinning microrobots generate controllable fluid flows powerful enough to manipulate passive objects from a distance.[1][2]

The technique, which the team calls fluidic torque-enabled manipulation, works by spinning disk-shaped microrobots — each roughly 300 micrometers in diameter — under an externally applied magnetic field. As the disks rotate in a liquid, they create circular flow patterns that exert torque on nearby objects. By adjusting the spin rate, the number of robots, and their spatial arrangement, the researchers tuned the generated torque to levels as high as 3.6 × 10⁻⁹ newton-meters.[2][1]

items.title: Flinders University scientists develop nano-cage that removes 98% of PFAS from water

featured_image.name: Nano-cage removes up to 98% of PFAS in tap water tests

items.description:
Researchers at Flinders University in South Australia have developed a nano-sized molecular cage that can remove more than 98 percent of toxic "forever chemicals" from tap water, offering a potential breakthrough in tackling one of the most persistent forms of water contamination worldwide.

The study, published in the journal Angewandte Chemie International Edition, details how the team led by Dr. Witold Bloch engineered a molecular cage that acts as a highly selective trap for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, known as PFAS. The method is notable for its ability to capture short-chain PFAS — smaller, more water-soluble variants that have long eluded conventional water treatment technologies.[1][2][3]

items.title: Ivory Coast to slash cocoa farmer prices in historic move

featured_image.name: Ivory Coast to announce cocoa mid-crop price by end of month ...

items.description:
Ivory Coast, the world's largest cocoa producer, will bring forward the start of its cocoa mid-crop season for the first time in history and sharply reduce prices paid to farmers, according to two government sources and two regulatory sources who spoke to Reuters. The move is designed to help the West African nation clear a growing pile of unsold cocoa that has accumulated at ports and inland storage sites in recent months.[1]

Under the plan, cocoa harvested beginning in March will be classified as mid-crop rather than main crop, with the farmer price set at between 800 and 1,000 CFA francs ($1.45 to $1.81) per kilogram — a steep drop from the current main crop rate of 2,800 CFA francs. The mid-crop traditionally begins in April and runs through September, but it will now start on March 1 and end a month earlier, in late August. The changes were approved by an interministerial committee overseeing raw materials last week.[2][3][1]

items.title: Rutgers study challenges theory that melting glaciers could slow climate change

featured_image.name: Antarctica's ice shelves could be melting faster than we thought

items.description:
Marine scientists at Rutgers University have found that meltwater from an Antarctic ice shelf delivers far less iron to the surrounding ocean than long assumed, upending a widely held theory that glacier-driven iron fertilization could act as a natural brake on climate change. The findings were published Tuesday in the journal Communications Earth and Environment.[1]

The theory posits that as rising temperatures cause Antarctic glaciers to melt, the iron released would nourish blooms of microscopic algae in the Southern Ocean. Those algae absorb carbon dioxide as they grow, theoretically pulling heat-trapping gas from the atmosphere. But direct sampling beneath the Dotson Ice Shelf in West Antarctica's Amundsen Sea has shown the mechanism is far weaker than models predicted.[2]

items.title: Oil holds near 7-month highs as US-Iran talks open in Geneva

featured_image.name: US-Iran talks live: Nuclear talks to kick off in Geneva amid ...

items.description:
Oil prices edged higher on Thursday, hovering near seven-month highs, as investors weighed whether a third round of nuclear talks between the United States and Iran could avert a military confrontation that threatens to disrupt crude supplies from the Middle East.

Brent crude futures traded near $71 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate held around $65.50, both largely flat after settling with minimal changes on Wednesday, according to Reuters. Brent had earlier in the week reached its highest level since late July as Washington continued to position military forces in the region to pressure Tehran into a deal.[1]
